claims.text: On 2024-08-05, Judge Amit Mehta of the US District Court for the District of Columbia ruled that Google held a monopoly in general search services and general search text advertising, violating Section 2 of the Sherman Act.
The court determined this status was maintained through default-distribution deals where Google paid billions to companies like Apple, Samsung, and Mozilla to be their default search engine.
Evidence showed Google spent about $26.3 billion on distribution in 2021 and paid Apple roughly 36% of Safari search-ad revenue.
This conduct created a self-reinforcing loop where defaults generated scale, which produced data, improved quality, and protected the default position against rivals.
On 2025-08-05 Judge Mehta ordered structural remedies requiring Google to sell Chrome, marking the first forced divestiture of a major tech company since the Microsoft case of 2000.
The court also prohibited future payments for default search placement through revenue-sharing agreements and imposed limits on acquisitions and AI-related investments.
Google appealed this decision to the DC Circuit in 2025 arguing that the ruling punished procompetitive innovation, leaving the final outcome pending as of 2025.
No evidence was retrieved this round.
